spn_trunk_walk.description:
Captain Vesk, Forsaken Rear Guard. This gate is the border and that road is the only reason the gate matters.

The Trunk Road runs from here to the Crossroads and on to the Sepulcher. Everything we have in Silverpine comes up it - orders, relief, the carts, the occasional person who actually knows something. Cut the road and this garrison isn't a border post, it's a building full of men in a wood.

Nobody has walked the whole length of it since the first frost. We patrol the first mile and the Sepulcher patrols their end and in between there is a stretch that exists on my map and nowhere else.

Walk it. All of it, to the Crossroads. Then come back and tell me what my map is wrong about.
spn_trunk_walk.accept_text: North up the Trunk Road, the whole length, to the Crossroads.
spn_trunk_walk.turn_in_text:
[Vesk marks three places on the map while you talk and does not like any of them.]

So it's passable. Passable, and watched.

That's worth knowing and I'd rather not have learned it. Thank you - you're the first man to give me that road in months.

spn_worg_cull.description:
Now you've walked it, you'll have seen the verge.

The worgs have moved onto it. Not into the road - the VERGE, the strip of scrub either side, where a thing can pace a cart for half a mile without ever being in the open. That's hunting behaviour and it's new this season.

And the ghouls have come in behind them, because a worg pack leaves a great deal behind and a ghoul is not proud. So now there are two problems on that strip, the second of which exists entirely because of the first.

Push them both back out of range of the road. Start with the worgs - take their leavings away and the ghouls will follow the food elsewhere.
spn_worg_cull.accept_text: Along the verge of the Trunk Road, both sides. Worgs first.
spn_worg_cull.turn_in_text:
Verge is clear enough to see across, which is all I ever ask of a verge.

That'll hold until the frost pushes them back down. By then I'd like to have a proper patrol on this stretch instead of borrowing passing strangers.

spn_pell_glands.description:
You'll be the one Vesk keeps sending into the woods. Good. Apothecary Pell - I have a requisition and no one to requisition.

Silverpine spider venom. Properly cut and properly reduced, I believe it can be made to SLOW the Plague rather than feed it, which is not a thing anyone in the Undercity wants to hear me say out loud.

I'll be honest with you, because you'll hear it from Vesk anyway: I have a great many theories. Most of them have been wrong. The difference with this one is that it can be tested with things that can be killed and weighed, rather than argued about in a chamber by people who have never cut anything.

Get me the glands. Intact, if you can manage it - a burst one is worth nothing but mess.
spn_pell_glands.accept_text: The spiders in the Silverpine woods. Intact glands, if you can manage it.
spn_pell_glands.turn_in_text:
Intact. All of them intact.

[He is already weighing one.]

Right. Now I can be wrong about this properly, with figures, instead of being wrong about it hopefully.

spn_ravenna_rite.description:
Dark Cleric Ravenna. Come closer - I won't raise my voice for this.

There is a woman at Olsen's Farthing called Marta. Her husband walks past her window. Every night, the same hour, the same track across the yard, and he does not come to the door and he does not go away, and she has been watching it for a year and a half.

I have prepared a Rite of Quieting. It will not bring him back and it will not punish him; it will let him stop. That's all it is, and that's all she asked for when she sent word.

I cannot leave this gate - I've tried, and Vesk is right to stop me. So you'll take it. And listen to me: do not read it aloud on the road. Not a line of it. The rite does not care where it is said.
spn_ravenna_rite.accept_text: To Widow Marta at Olsen's Farthing. And do not read it aloud on the way.
spn_ravenna_rite.turn_in_text:
[Marta holds the scroll without unrolling it.]

He was a good walker. That's a stupid thing to say about a man but it's what I keep thinking - he walked everywhere, he'd walk to the Sepulcher for a nail rather than wait for the cart.

I'll say it tonight at the hour he comes. Thank you for carrying it. And thank the cleric, and tell her I did ask - that nobody made me.

spn_scout_survey.description:
Don't stand in the road. Here, in the verge, where the ground's soft - that's why I'm standing in it.

Look at this. And this. Fresh tracks, three spurs off the Trunk Road, all within a fortnight: the east road to the Dead Field, the path up to the Shadowspring Pools, and the lane into Malden's Orchard.

Three spurs is a pattern. One spur is somebody taking a short cut; three is somebody mapping a wood. And every one of these goes OFF the road and doesn't come back onto it where I can see.

I want eyes on the far end of each. Not the middles - the ends. Walk them to where they stop and tell me what's standing there.
spn_scout_survey.accept_text: Three spurs: the Dead Field road, the Shadowspring path, the Orchard lane. Walk them to the end.
spn_scout_survey.turn_in_text:
All three ending somewhere occupied. I'd half hoped you'd come back and tell me I was reading deer.

I'll take this to Vesk tonight. He'll want it as three separate problems and I'm going to make him look at it as one.

spn_farthing_hounds.description:
Mind the fence. Don't put your hand on the fence.

Gaffer Olsen. I kept hounds here for forty years - good ones, working dogs, and I'd have told anybody who asked that I knew every one of them better than I knew most people.

Since the plague they've kept ME. They pace that fence all night. They don't bark; they pace, and they stop when I come to the window, and they wait for me to go back to bed. And the risen hands open the gate for them, which they do because opening the gate was their job and nobody's told them the farm's finished.

I'm an old man who is frightened of his own dogs and I'll say that out loud rather than dress it up. Deal with the hands, and deal with the pack.
spn_farthing_hounds.accept_text: The pack at the fence line, and the risen hands who keep opening the gate.
spn_farthing_hounds.turn_in_text:
Quiet yard.

I slept. First full night since the plague came through - I'd forgotten what it does to a man's thinking to get a whole one.

spn_olsens_seed.description:
Now. Something that isn't killing, if you can stand it.

The hands are carrying the seed. Still. In their coat pockets, same as they did when there was sowing to do - a sack each, because that was how my father ran it and I never saw reason to change it.

I want it back. I want to put one row in, up the near side where the drainage is decent, and I want to see whether anything comes up.

I know what you're thinking and you'd be right. Nothing's grown in Silverpine soil since the plague. But I've got a season's worth of nothing to do and a farm that's stopped being a farm, and one row is the difference between a man who's finished and a man who's waiting to find out.
spn_olsens_seed.accept_text: The risen hands carry the sacks in their coat pockets, same as in life.
spn_olsens_seed.turn_in_text:
[He opens a sack and runs it through his fingers.]

Dry. Dry's the main thing. Dry seed keeps.

I'll put the row in on Thursday. Come back in the spring and we'll both find out together.

spn_old_hob.description:
There's one more and I've been putting it off since you got here.

Hob leads the pack. He's the oldest dog I ever had and he was the best of them - not the quickest, not the keenest nose, but the one you could leave with the stock and the one the children could pull about. He slept under that bench. You can still see where he wore the grass away.

He's out past the top gate now and the rest follow him, and I've had a season of telling myself that means something's left in him. It doesn't. I've watched him work the fence and there's nothing in it that was my dog.

Don't make it slow. That's the whole of what I'm asking.
spn_old_hob.accept_text: Past the top gate. He leads them. Don't make it slow.
spn_old_hob.turn_in_text:
[Olsen is sitting on the bench when you come back.]

Quick, then. Good.

Forty years of dogs and that one was the best of them. I'll have him under the bench where he used to lie. He's earned a spot a damn sight more than I have.

spn_farmhand_locket.description:
A silver locket, pried out of the coat pocket of a risen farmhand - carried the way the seed sacks are carried, because carrying it was simply what he did.

It opens stiffly. There's no portrait inside, only a name scratched into the metal in a hand that was not a craftsman's:

Marta.

And under the name, folded small and gone brittle, a lock of hair. Grey-brown. The same colour as the woman's at Olsen's Farthing, who has a husband that walks past her window at the same hour every night and never comes to the door.
spn_farmhand_locket.accept_text: Take it to Widow Marta at Olsen's Farthing.
spn_farmhand_locket.turn_in_text:
[She takes it in both hands and sits down on the step.]

He scratched that himself. He had no hand for letters and he wouldn't let the smith do it, said it wouldn't count.

He was carrying it. All this time, out there, carrying it in the same pocket.

I'll say the cleric's rite tonight. And I'll have this on when I do, and he can go, and I'll know that whatever was still walking out there had hold of the right thing.

spn_rh_husks.description:
Keeper Oswin. You'll have to forgive the state of me - I've been digging since before light.

I have buried the same corpse three times this month. The same one. I know his face, I know which plot, and three times I have filled that hole in and three times he has been standing beside it in the morning with the soil off him.

The husks come up all over the back plots. Faster than I can fill, which means I am no longer a gravekeeper, I am a man moving earth in a circle.

Thin them out for me. Give me one clear day. If I can get a full day's work done without it undoing itself behind me, I'll know this ground can still be kept.
spn_rh_husks.accept_text: The back plots, where the soil's turned. Give me one clear day.
spn_rh_husks.turn_in_text:
A whole day. I filled nine and not one of them came back up.

[He looks at his hands.]

I'd stopped believing that was possible, which is a dangerous thing for a man in my trade to stop believing.

spn_rh_moss.description:
Acolyte Dessa. Don't tread on the markers - not for reverence, for the moss.

Look at it. It only grows on the mourning stones. Not the walls, not the trees, not the ground between - the stones, and only the ones with names still legible on them, which is the detail that has kept me awake.

I think it feeds the dead. Or they feed it. I have the two possibilities written out and I cannot get further than that from the outside, because the creepers that tend it will not let me near a stone long enough to cut a clean sample.

Bring me clippings from the creepers themselves. Whatever they've been taking in is in them, and I would very much like to know what this cemetery has been eating.
spn_rh_moss.accept_text: Off the grave moss creepers, not the stones. I want what's inside them.
spn_rh_moss.turn_in_text:
[She has three of them open before you've finished speaking.]

It's the same in all of them. Whatever this is, it isn't local to a plot, it's local to the HILL.

I'll need to say that to Oswin carefully. He has spent twenty years believing this is a graveyard with a problem, and I am about to suggest it's a problem with a graveyard on it.

spn_rh_vigil.description:
I need to ask you for something tedious and a little frightening, and I'll not pretend otherwise.

Something is lifting the dead on this hill. Not raising - LIFTING, from below, and if I knew where they were climbing from I'd know what I'm arguing with. The three oldest crypts are the only points on this hill where you can hear the under-ground properly.

So: stand at each one. Stand still, and listen, long enough to be certain of what you're hearing. That's all it is.

I've asked three people. None of them came back with an answer. Two came back.
spn_rh_vigil.accept_text: The three oldest crypts. Stand at each and listen. Properly - it takes time.
spn_rh_vigil.turn_in_text:
[Dessa listens to your description without interrupting once.]

Same sound at all three. Which means it isn't coming from a crypt at all - it's coming from under the whole hill and they're the places thin enough to hear it.

Thank you. And I'm sorry - I'd hoped very much that you'd come back and tell me it was water.

spn_rh_watchman.description:
There's one walking the upper cemetery and I'd rather you heard about him from me.

He's one of ours. A Forsaken watchman, posted here when Raven Hill still had a posting, and he has never stopped doing his rounds. Same route, same hours.

He doesn't answer a challenge any more. I've tried. And about a month ago I used his name - properly, the whole thing, the way you'd call to a man across a yard - and he turned and looked at me and there was nothing behind it, and then he carried on walking.

I knew him. He was better company than anyone else they ever sent up here. I'm not going to watch him walk that route through another winter.
spn_rh_watchman.accept_text: The upper cemetery, on his round. He won't answer you either.
spn_rh_watchman.turn_in_text:
[Oswin takes a long time over it.]

I'll put him up by the wall where he used to stop and look at the valley. He always stopped there. Every round, same spot, and I never once asked him what he was looking at.

That's the part I'll be chewing on. Not the rest of it. That.

spn_df_crows.description:
Take it. Go on - it's a good bow, it's a better bow than I deserve, and I can't use it any more.

Huntress Verrel. I have been trying to shoot the crows of the Dead Field for a week.

They don't die the way crows die. I hit them. I KNOW I hit them - I've hit a bird at twice that distance in worse light every season since I was fourteen. They take it, and they look at me, and then they settle on the next fence-post down and wait for me to try again.

I've started flinching. That's why you're getting the bow. A hunter who's begun to flinch is no use to anybody until she's seen somebody else do it right.

Go and clear the fence line. I'll watch, and then I'd like the bow back.
spn_df_crows.accept_text: The fence line along the Dead Field. Take the bow - I've stopped trusting it.
spn_df_crows.turn_in_text:
[She takes the bow back and checks the string out of pure habit.]

So it was the birds.

That's the best news I've had in a fortnight. I can work with a wrong bird. I was starting to think I'd have to go home.

spn_df_harrowers.description:
You'll have to come up to the loft if you want to talk. I don't go down after dark.

Tobb. I worked this field - last one out when it went bad, first one back when I couldn't stand being anywhere else, which I know says something about me and I'd rather it wasn't said.

The scarecrows walk. I've watched them from this window for weeks: they come down off the posts at dark and they go up and down the furrows the way we used to walk them, and at first light they're back on the frames.

I'm not frightened of them, quite. It's that they're doing it RIGHT. The spacing, the turns at the headland. Somebody taught them that and the only people who knew it are the ones who used to work here.

Get them out of the furrows.
spn_df_harrowers.accept_text: In the furrows after dark. They work the rows the way we used to.
spn_df_harrowers.turn_in_text:
I came down. First time after dark since the spring.

Stood in the middle of the field and there was nothing in it but me. That's what I wanted and it's a good deal lonelier than I'd thought through.

spn_df_straw.description:
One more thing, and then I'll let you go, and I'd ask you to be careful how you look at me while I say it.

Every harrower has a charm sewn inside its coat. Straw, bound in a cross, the old kind people put up for a good harvest. My wife made them. She made one for every hand on this farm every spring and she was teased about it for years.

I know the stitching. I'd know it anywhere - she went round the outside twice and back through the middle and nobody else in Silverpine does it that way.

Bring the charms back to me. I don't want them in those coats. I want them somewhere decent, where what she meant by them is still what they mean.
spn_df_straw.accept_text: Sewn inside the harrowers' coats. I'll know the stitching.
spn_df_straw.turn_in_text:
[He goes through them one at a time, feeling the backs.]

All hers.

I'll put them in the barn above the door, which is where she'd have hung them anyway if anyone had let her. And then I think I might go and stay at the Crossroads a while.

I've done what I came back to do. I'd got it into my head that I had to keep doing it forever.

spn_df_ring.description:
A gold band, tarnished to brown, pecked out of a crow's nest in the fence line and dropped in the stubble.

It is a plain thing. No stones, no pattern - the sort of ring bought by somebody who had been saving for it rather than choosing it.

The inside is engraved, worn soft but perfectly legible:

T. & L., forever.

There is a farmhand sleeping in the Dead Field barn who gave his initial to half the stories in this valley, and a wife he does not talk about except by her stitching.
spn_df_ring.accept_text: Take it up to Tobb in the Dead Field barn.
spn_df_ring.turn_in_text:
[Tobb turns it over without putting it on.]

Lenna. She lost it in the harvest the year before the plague and we went through that stubble on our hands and knees for two days.

She said a crow had it. I said crows don't take gold, they take shine, and she said that was the same thing to a crow and I was being difficult.

[He closes his hand around it.]

She was right. She was usually right. Thank you.

spn_df_king.description:
Now I'll tell you what I was really doing out here with a bow I'd stopped trusting.

There's one in the field that rules the rest. Taller than a man, straw crown on it, wrapped up in a farmer's shroud - and the others take their timing from it. I've watched the whole field turn at the headland because that thing turned.

I've shot it twice. Both good hits, both in it, and it did not go down and it did not get angry. It looked at me, properly looked, for about as long as it takes to decide something.

And it's been coming a little closer to this fence every night since.

I'd rather not be the thing it decided about. Put it down.
spn_df_king.accept_text: Out in the deep furrows. It wears a straw crown and it's been watching me.
spn_df_king.turn_in_text:
[Verrel lets out a breath she looks like she's been holding for a fortnight.]

It stayed down.

I'll sleep in the open tonight, out by the fence, just to prove to myself I can. And tomorrow I'm going to shoot something ordinary and enjoy it enormously.

spn_gate_hold.description:
Gatewarden Ilsa. State your business or stand aside - no, don't, I can see what you are. Come here, you're useful.

This is the iron door of the Sepulcher. The dead are welcome through it. That's the whole point of the place and I've no quarrel with anyone who walks up and asks.

My quarrel is with what follows them. The treants have come down off the ridge and the ghouls come in behind, and between them the approach has become a thing you have to FIGHT your way along to reach a door that was built to be open.

I've held this gate a long time and I have never once had to tell a newly risen soul to run the last stretch. Clear the approach.
spn_gate_hold.accept_text: On the approach to the iron door. Treants off the ridge, ghouls behind them.
spn_gate_hold.turn_in_text:
Approach is walkable.

Two came in this evening on their own feet, slowly, looking at everything the way they do. That's how it's supposed to go. That's the entire job.

spn_orchard_blight.description:
Malwick, orchard-warden. It's a title I keep using because the alternative is admitting what I actually am now, which is a man who walked to the Sepulcher to ask for help with some apples.

Malden's Orchard hasn't borne fruit in years. The trees still DROP, mind. Brown stuff, heavy, comes down in the night - and then it moves. It gets up off the grass and goes about the rows.

That's the shamblers. And where the windfall piles up and rots, the wasps have hived in it, so now you cannot clear the one without going through the other. I've tried both orders.

Get the shamblers out of the rows and the wasps out of the rot. Then I can at least walk my own orchard, which is more than I've managed since spring.
spn_orchard_blight.accept_text: Through the rows. Shamblers off the grass, and the wasps hived in the windfall.
spn_orchard_blight.turn_in_text:
I walked the long row. Both ways, no stick.

You'll think that's a small thing. I planted the long row.

spn_orchard_cores.description:
[He sets a cut rotapple on the table between you.]

Look at it, if you've the stomach. There, at the middle.

That's a seed-core. Rotapple, black all through, dense as a stone and WARM. Not warm from the sun; I've taken them out at first light in frost and they were warm then.

Every shambler has one. Which means they aren't rotting fruit that learned to walk - they're being SEEDED, and whatever's doing the seeding is putting something into each one that holds its heat.

Bring me the cores. There's a furnace at the end of the orchard that hasn't been lit since Malden's day, and I intend to light it, and I intend to put every one of them in it and stand there until they're ash.
spn_orchard_cores.accept_text: At the heart of each shambler. Black, dense, and warm - you'll feel it.
spn_orchard_cores.turn_in_text:
[The furnace is already roaring when you get back.]

In they go.

Listen to that. They're SPITTING. Whatever's in those was never going to come out of that orchard on its own.

spn_orchard_keeper.description:
Under the big tree at the back. You'll have seen it and taken it for stump-work.

That was Malden's gardener. Forty years on that ground, knew every tree by name - and I mean that literally, he'd named them, he had names for trees and he'd use them in conversation and look at you as if you were the strange one.

He's still working. That's what you need to understand before you go down there. He prunes. He clears windfall. He tends the blight the way he used to tend the crop, with exactly the same care, because as far as anything left in him is concerned the orchard is producing beautifully.

[A thin smile.] He always did love his work.
spn_orchard_keeper.accept_text: Under the big tree at the back of the orchard. He's still tending it.
spn_orchard_keeper.turn_in_text:
[Malwick doesn't go and look.]

I'll put him at the foot of the long row. He'd want to be in the ground out there, and now at least the ground can have him instead of the other way round.

And then I've a proposition for you, if you've the legs for a mountain.

spn_pools_beasts.description:
Yaelis. Pools warden, and before you ask, yes, that was once a real posting. I've come down to the Sepulcher because a warden with no pools left to keep isn't much use up there.

The Shadowspring Pools were a drinking-hole. Forsaken went up there, stood at the water, and had an hour to themselves; there's not much the risen want, but there's something about standing by water that a good many of us still do.

Then the springs turned black, and the bog beasts came into the shallows, and the crocolisks came in after them. Now nobody stands at my pools at all.

I'd settle for making the near bank safe enough to stand beside. That's not a strategic objective and I'm aware of it. Clear the shallows anyway.
spn_pools_beasts.accept_text: In the shallows on the near bank. Bog beasts first - the crocolisks follow them in.
spn_pools_beasts.turn_in_text:
Somebody told me they went up this evening and stood at the water for the better part of an hour.

Didn't say anything to me. Didn't need to. That's the posting.

spn_pools_fangs.description:
Something you can actually be paid for, since I can't pay you.

The Rot Hide slitherers work the pools' edge, and their fangs carry a venom the Apothecary Society has standing coin out for. Properly standing coin - they'll take as many as anyone brings and they've never once asked where from.

I want them drained for my own reasons, which are that a slitherer has taken two of my patrol in a year and I am not a big enough person to pretend that's professional detachment.

So: you get the Society's coin, I get the pools' edge quieter, and the slitherers get what they've got coming. I find that an unusually tidy arrangement.
spn_pools_fangs.accept_text: Shadowspring Pools, east of here. The slitherers work the edge, and the Society pays for the fangs.
spn_pools_fangs.turn_in_text:
Good. Drained and bagged.

Take the lot to the Society and don't let them tell you the rate's dropped. It hasn't. They say that to everyone who looks like they've walked a long way.

spn_muckmaw.description:
The deep pool. The one at the back that doesn't reflect anything.

There's something in it. Old - older than the springs turning, I think, and that's not a thing I say lightly. It took Hest in the spring and it took Dorn in the autumn, and both times there was no struggle at all. They were at the bank and then they were not at the bank.

The locals call it Muckmaw, which makes it sound like a story for children, and I have let them keep calling it that because the alternative is explaining to a patrol that there is something in my pools that eats a Forsaken without waking the water.

Kill it. I've run out of scouts and patience in roughly that order.
spn_muckmaw.accept_text: Shadowspring Pools. It's in the deep pool at the back, the one with no reflection.
spn_muckmaw.turn_in_text:
[Yaelis stands at the deep pool's edge for a long moment, which she has not done in a year.]

It reflects.

I'd never once seen the bottom of that. There's a cart down there. A whole cart, and I have no idea how long it's been in my pools.

spn_sd_skitterers.description:
When you go into the Skittering Dark, keep to the middle of the path and don't put a hand out to steady yourself. Everything in there that looks like a branch is a decision.

Corvane, webhunter. I've worked the Skittering Dark for months and I'll tell you what's changed, because it's changed fast: they're bigger, they're bolder, and they've started drifting toward the Trunk Road.

That last one is what matters. A spider in a wood is a spider in a wood. A spider on a supply road is a Sepulcher problem with my name on the report.

Cull the breeding stock - the big skitterers and the full-grown ones. Take them before the swarm rather than after, because after is a different conversation entirely.
spn_sd_skitterers.accept_text: Deep in the Skittering Dark. The breeding stock, not the small ones.
spn_sd_skitterers.turn_in_text:
That's a dent in the next generation.

They'll breed it back if we stop. That's the whole miserable arithmetic of this wood - you don't win, you just stay ahead.

spn_sd_sacs.description:
Now the part that actually ends it, rather than postponing it.

The skitterers carry their egg sacs with them. They don't nest them and they don't leave them - they carry them, which is why nobody has ever found a chamber to burn and why everyone who's tried to clear that wood has failed doing it the sensible way.

Take the sacs off them. All you can carry.

And here's the other thing, and it's why I want them rather than just destroyed in place: the Widow's brood will follow a sac. They'll follow it a long way. A man holding enough of them can make something in this wood listen to him, and I have an idea about that which I'm not ready to say out loud yet.
spn_sd_sacs.accept_text: The Skittering Dark, east of here. They carry the sacs on them. Bring back what you can.
spn_sd_sacs.turn_in_text:
[He stows them with a great deal more care than he's shown anything else.]

Good. That's the next generation in a bag instead of in the wood.

Don't ask me yet. Ask me after Longleg.

spn_sd_longleg.description:
Longleg. That's the one that takes a hunter a week.

Size of a cart. I want you to hold that in your head rather than nodding past it, because everyone nods past it and then they see it and they stop thinking clearly at exactly the wrong moment.

It doesn't web. It stalks - properly stalks, matches your pace, stays off the path, and comes when you've stopped moving and started looking at something else. I've got three apprentices' worth of experience in that sentence and I'd rather not get a fourth.

It'll be on the high ground off the Skittering road. Go slowly, don't stop in the open, and don't look at anything for long.
spn_sd_longleg.accept_text: The Skittering Dark, on the high ground off its road. It stalks, so don't stop in the open.
spn_sd_longleg.turn_in_text:
[Corvane sits down on the path, which in this wood is not something he does.]

Three apprentices.

I'll take their kit down to the Crossroads and send it on. I've been carrying it in my pack for a year because sending it felt like finishing something.

spn_sd_lair.description:
Here's the idea I wasn't ready to say.

Longleg came from somewhere. So did everything else in there - the size of them, the boldness, all of it starting at once a few months back. That's not a wood changing its mind, that's a brood with a mother in it.

There's a cave at the end of the Skittering road. The Widow's Lair, if you listen to the Crossroads carters. I've been to within sight of the mouth twice and turned back both times, and I'd like to stop pretending that was judgement.

Stand at the mouth. Don't go in - I mean that, don't go in. Tell me how deep the webs run and whether there's air moving out of it.
spn_sd_lair.accept_text: The cave at the end of the Skittering road. Stand at the mouth. Do NOT go in.
spn_sd_lair.turn_in_text:
Air coming out of it. Warm air.

[He is quiet for a while.]

Then it isn't a cave, it's a way through to something, and this wood has been getting its weather from somewhere other than the sky.

That's beyond a webhunter. That goes to Vesk, and Vesk will send it on, and somebody with a better title than either of us can decide what to do about it.

spn_rg_reckoning.description:
Stand there a moment. I want to do this properly.

Four reports on this desk. The Watchman is down - Oswin's man, who'd been walking that round since before I had this post. The Scarecrow-King is down. The Orchardkeeper is down. Muckmaw is down, and I had a standing order about Muckmaw that I'd stopped expecting anyone to action.

Four threads through these pines, and every one of them was somebody's year. Oswin's, Verrel's, Malwick's, Yaelis's. They've all written to me separately and not one of them mentioned the others, because none of them knew there was a pattern. I'm the only one who sees all four, and that's the only useful thing about this desk.

So: thank you. From this garrison, and from four people who'll never put it together.
spn_rg_reckoning.accept_text: Come and stand at Captain Vesk's desk at the border gate.
spn_rg_reckoning.turn_in_text:
[He actually stands up.]

That's the Rear Guard's thanks, and it's worth exactly what the Rear Guard is worth, which these days is not much.

But these pines are quieter than they were when you came up that road, and I keep the map, and the map says so.

spn_orchard_graft.description:
Here's my proposition, and I've had two seasons to be sure of it.

Every tree in that orchard is rotted at the root. Every one. I have dug up four to be certain, including the long row, and there is nothing to be reversed - the blight isn't in the fruit, it's in the ground, and the ground is going nowhere.

But the wood ABOVE it is still clean in places. High boughs, new growth, the parts that never touched soil. You can take cuttings from clean wood and graft them onto living stock, and they'll be the same trees - Malden's own stock, still fruiting somewhere.

The nearest living orchard is over the range, in Hillsbrad. It's a long way and there's a mountain in it.

I'm too old to carry them and too stubborn to let them die out there. Take them.
